title: Converting Nominal to Real
short: Divide a dollar amount by the price index over 100 to compare dollars from different years.
trouble: Students compare wages or prices from different decades in nominal dollars, or multiply by the index when they should divide.

blocks.html: Is a \$15 hourly wage today better than \$10 an hour twenty years ago? It depends on how much prices rose in between. The Inflation, Deflation and Disinflation and the price index let you compare dollars from different years.

To express an amount in base-year dollars, divide by the index over 100: $$\text{real value} = \dfrac{\text{nominal value}}{\text{index}/100}$$ To move an amount from year A's dollars into year B's dollars: $$\text{amount}_B = \text{amount}_A \times \dfrac{\text{index}_B}{\text{index}_A}$$

An index of 150 means prices are 1.5 times base-year prices. So a \$30 wage at that time buys what \$20 bought in the base year: $30 \div 1.5 = 20$. Dividing takes the price rise out. Multiplying instead would put a second dose of inflation in, making the old wage look even bigger, which is backwards. The ratio form works the same way: it scales by how much prices changed between the two years.

blocks.cap: Hourly wages from three years, as paid (gold) and in the dollars of the year you choose (green). Switch the year: the comparison among the green bars never changes.

blocks.title: Base-year dollars
blocks.q: A worker earns \$48,000. The price index is 120. What is the salary in base-year dollars?
steps: The salary buys what \$40,000 bought in the base year.

blocks.title: Then and now
blocks.q: A movie ticket cost \$4 in 1990, when the index was 130. The index is 260 today. What is the 1990 price in today's dollars?
steps: If tickets now cost more than \$8, they rose faster than prices in general.

blocks.title: Did the raise keep up?
blocks.q: A wage went from \$15 (index 100) to \$18 (index 125). Did the real wage rise?
steps: $14.40 < 15$: the real wage fell, even though the paycheck number grew 20%.

blocks.html: Comparing amounts from different decades in nominal dollars, or multiplying by the index when you should divide. Check the direction: if prices rose since year A, an old amount should become a bigger number in today's dollars, and a recent amount a smaller number in old dollars.
